IN
THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

McDermott v. McDermott,

2013 BCSC 534

Date: 20130321

Docket: E012183

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Susan Dawn McDermott

Plaintiff

And

Kevin Franklin McDermott

Defendant

Corrected Judgment:  The front page of
the judgment was corrected on April 4, 2013

Before: The Honourable Mr. Justice
Walker

Oral Reasons
for Judgment

Counsel
for the Plaintiff:

J. Maynard

The
Defendant, appearing in person on his own behalf:

K.F. McDermott

Place
and Date of Trial:

Vancouver, B.C.

February 12-15, 2013

February 18-22, 2013

February 25-March 1, 2013

March 4-8, 2013

March 11-13, 2013

March 18-21, 2013

Place
and Date of Judgment:

Vancouver, B.C.

March 21, 2013

I.          Introduction

[
1
]

These
reasons for judgment concern competing mid-trial applications brought by both
parties after the fifth week of trial.

[
2
]

Mr. Kevin
McDermott, the defendant, seeks orders for production of further documents from
his former spouse, the plaintiff, Ms. Susan McDermott, including documents over
which solicitor and client privilege has been asserted. Ms. McDermott now
refers to herself as Ms. Harrington and I will do likewise in these
reasons for judgment. Ms. Harrington seeks an order declaring a mistrial.

[
3
]

Mr. McDermott
seeks production of three broad categories of documents. His application was
conducted as a
voir dire
.

[
4
]

The first
category of documents concerns communications between Ms. Harrington and Mr. Maynard,
her counsel from Prince Edward Island who represents her on the instant
applications and at trial. Mr. McDermott claims that he found these communications
with her lawyer following the inadvertent disclosure of non-privileged email communications
with her sister on November 12, 2012. In one of those communications, Ms. Harrington
told her sister about a plan to be undertaken by her lawyer, on her behalf,
that would cause an application to be lost in this Court in order to facilitate
an appeal to purposely delay the trial.

[
5
]

Mr. McDermott
says that their plan was to manipulate the process of the courts to secure
certain advantages for Ms. Harrington. Mr. McDermott characterizes
the plan (spoken of in the emails) as an abuse of the Court’s process; as such,
he says that communications concerning it cannot be privileged because they
fall within the crime-fraud exception to privilege.

[
6
]

Mr. McDermott
also says that the communications concerning that plan are relevant to the
issues to be determined at trial and must be produced. According to Mr. McDermott,
those communications constitute a further example of Ms. Harrington’s ongoing
attempt since at least 2003 to obstruct and delay these proceedings so that his
access in British Columbia to his teenage children, who are living in Prince
Edward Island with Ms. Harrington, will be impeded wherever possible. Mr. McDermott
describes a persistent and deliberate course of conduct taken by Ms. Harrington
over the course of years to ignore or otherwise fail to abide by orders of this
Court.

[
7
]

Furthermore,
he asserts that the plan evidenced in these email communications is also relevant
to his claim that Ms. Harrington has engaged in ongoing alienation of the
children towards him and further, that it affects the nature and scope of the
access regime that will be determined at trial and who should pay for it.

[
8
]

Lastly,
Mr. McDermott says that the communications in respect of the plan are also
relevant to his contempt application brought against Ms. Harrington for
failing to deliver answers to interrogatories ordered by the Court on May 22,
2012. The contempt application is being heard contemporaneously with the trial.

[
9
]

The second
category of documents sought by Mr. McDermott are those concerning matters
raised in solicitor and client communications over which he says Ms. Harrington
has intentionally waived privilege during the course of this proceeding,
including the trial.

[
10
]

The
documents falling in the third category are those that Mr. McDermott says
are: in the possession, custody, or control of Ms. Harrington; relevant to
the issues to be determined at trial; and not protected by privilege.
Accordingly, his position is that they ought to have been disclosed. Mr. McDermott
asserts that Ms. Harrington has intentionally suppressed the disclosure of
some of those documents.

[
11
]

Ms. Harrington
denies that she devised and then participated in any plan to abuse the Court’s
process. In her application, she seeks an order declaring a mistrial and
injunctive relief against Mr. McDermott to prevent him from pursuing her
for the claims he advances in this proceeding.

[
12
]

Ms. Harrington
claims that Mr. McDermott “hacked” his way into her email account and
surreptitiously (and perhaps illegally) viewed her emails and took copies of
some of them. Her position is that Mr. McDermott has reviewed many, if not
all, of her communications with Mr. Maynard that include their trial
strategy. Accordingly, Ms. Harrington’s application is grounded on what
she characterizes as Mr. McDermott’s grave misconduct and what she asserts
to be resulting prejudice that is so adverse to her rights that it cannot be
remedied by any other terms.

[
13
]

Before
giving my reasons, I would like to make two remarks about the hearing of the
applications. First, both parties agreed to the other’s request to submit to
cross-examination in court on their various affidavits. Second, notwithstanding
the very serious nature of the allegations concerning the manipulation of the Court’s
process levelled against her and her counsel, Ms. Harrington chose to be
represented by Mr. Maynard. Both Ms. Harrington and Mr. Maynard
were aware well before the hearing that I would not permit Mr. Maynard to
proffer evidence about his role in any of the impugned matters in the guise of
submissions.

II.          Background

[
14
]

Some
background concerning earlier conflict between the parties is necessary to
provide context to the applications.

[
15
]

The
original trial concerning the matrimonial issues between the parties, including
issues of guardianship and access, was conducted before Mr. Justice Lowry
(as he then was) in December 2002. His reasons for judgment were issued on
January 8, 2003:
2003 BCSC 38
. Custody was awarded to Ms. Harrington (without
opposition from Mr. McDermott at trial); joint guardianship was also
ordered. Mr. McDermott’s access to his children was the significant issue to
be determined given that the children would continue to live with their mother (at
that time, they resided in Moncton, New Brunswick, and Mr. McDermott lived
in Vancouver).

[
16
]

Ms. Harrington
unsuccessfully opposed access to Mr. McDermott in British Columbia. Lowry
J. ordered an access regime that included specific terms requiring the children
to spend time with their father in Vancouver - specifically, no more than two
trips to Vancouver by the children per year and access in Moncton (if sufficient
notice was provided): paras. 9 – 12.

[
17
]

Lowry
J. also ordered that Mr. McDermott was required to provide notice to Ms. Harrington
of his intention to exercise access in British Columbia and that she would have
an opportunity to object, so that any dispute could be determined on
application to the Court. In addition, Lowry J. ordered that Mr. McDermott
bear the costs of transporting the children to Vancouver and that if Ms. Harrington
wished to accompany the children, then she would be responsible for her own
costs.

[
18
]

The
access regime ordered by Lowry J. quickly degenerated into a series of disputes
between the parties. Multiple applications, including contempt applications,
were filed and then argued before at least six judges of this Court between
2003 and 2009. Ms. Harrington filed various applications to vary the terms
of access in order to block Mr. McDermott’s access in British Columbia. She
was unsuccessful. Further history concerning some of those applications and the
ongoing issues between the parties is set out in the reasons for judgment
issued by Romilly J. at
2004 BCSC 59
and by Holmes J. (November 26, 2004),
Vancouver E012183 (B.C.S.C.). Holmes J. varied the access regime to refine the
mechanism by which Mr. McDermott would provide notice for access and Ms. Harrington
could object. She continued to hear further applications from the parties on an
ongoing basis through to 2007.

[
19
]

In the
meantime, in 2005, Ms. Harrington filed an application before the Prince
Edward Island Supreme Court (originally brought on an
ex parte
basis) to
vary the access regime previously ordered by this Court. She sought to confine Mr. McDermott’s
access to the Maritimes and to limit its duration, thus preventing his access
to the children in British Columbia. But Ms. Harrington failed to advise
the Prince Edward Supreme Court of the ongoing proceedings before this Court
when she brought that application. Once the Prince Edward Island Supreme Court
learned of the ongoing proceedings before this Court, her application was
dismissed by Jenkins J. on September 15, 2005. An excerpt taken from his
reasons for judgment can be
found at
2010 BCSC 531
at para.
17
.

[
20
]

Following
Ms. Harrington’s unsuccessful application before the Prince Edward Island
Supreme Court, the Court of Appeal issued reasons for judgment from an appeal
brought by Mr. McDermott from a decision issued by Holmes J. on April 4,
2007:
2008 BCCA 166
. Chief Justice Finch ordered that the determination of an
appropriate access regime, and who should pay for it, be remitted to trial.

[
21
]

The
parties appear to have negotiated a settlement agreement in 2008 (“2008
Agreement”) concerning access and the costs of it, plus Mr. McDermott’s
obligations for child and spousal support. The question of whether an
enforceable agreement was made in 2008 is a live issue in the ongoing trial
between the parties. Even if one was reached, not all of its terms appear to
have been adhered to.

[
22
]

Before
the trial ordered by the Court of Appeal could get underway, Ms. Harrington
brought an application in this Court in the first quarter of 2010 seeking an
order transferring to the Prince Edward Island Supreme Court that part of the
proceedings concerning custody of and access to the children (“transfer
application”). The transfer application was heard and dismissed on March 19,
2010:
2010 BCSC 531
.

III.        The New Trial Concerning
Access

[
23
]

The new
trial commenced in July 2010, but did not finish due to the parties’
insufficient estimate of trial time. More importantly, it became apparent
during the trial that both parties wished to make further allegations against
each other that had not been pleaded. As a result, I ordered the parties to
deliver new pleadings that were to contain all of the allegations they wished
to advance.

[
24
]

Those
new pleadings were eventually filed by late 2011. Mr. McDermott filed a counterclaim
pleading that Ms. Harrington had alienated the children from him. Ms. Harrington
sought an order that Mr. McDermott contribute to future but not past extraordinary
expenses and an order varying a previous order of the Court that he pay child
support in a specified amount. She also sought to vary a prior order concerning
the access regime. The trial was then re-scheduled to continue on July 9,
2012.

[
25
]

It is
important to understand for one of the issues to be determined at trial (i.e., the
question of who should pay the costs of bringing the children from Prince
Edward Island to and from Vancouver on an ongoing basis) that Ms. Harrington
changed her position days before the trial resumed on July 9. She withdrew her
longstanding consent to pay one-half of the access, in part because of what she
claims is Mr. McDermott’s inappropriate conduct. She now seeks an order
that Mr. McDermott pay for all of the costs of access. At trial, she has
sought to castigate Mr. McDermott for failing to pay spousal and child
support in accordance with a prior order of this Court and the 2008 Agreement. In
addition, after the trial was adjourned in July 2010, Mr. Maynard
threatened to bring contempt proceedings on behalf of Ms. Harrington
against Mr. McDermott for failing to pay child support pursuant to the
2008 Agreement.

[
26
]

Ms. Harrington’s
castigation of Mr. McDermott puts squarely in issue the terms of the 2008
Agreement, which was made after the impugned child support order was made. On
the face of some of the documents in evidence, the 2008 Agreement purports to
waive all of Ms. Harrington’s claims for spousal support and to define Mr. McDermott’s
obligation for child support. One issue to be determined at trial is whether
the parties were
ad idem
so that an enforceable agreement was reached;
another is whether the 2008 Agreement, assuming the parties concluded a binding
agreement, defined Mr. McDermott’s obligation to pay child support in an
unambiguous way.

[
27
]

Because
of a successful pre-trial application brought by Ms. Harrington, her claim
for future extraordinary expenses was included in the list of issues to be
determined at the trial.

[
28
]

The
parties later agreed that Ms. Harrington’s application to vary child
support will be heard by application following the determination of the issues at
trial.

IV.       Mr. McDermott’s Disclosure
Application

[
29
]

I
propose to first deal with the disclosure application brought by Mr. McDermott
because some of my findings affect my analysis of Ms. Harrington’s
mistrial application.

[
30
]

As I
have said, Mr. McDermott seeks disclosure of three broad categories of
documents, namely:

(a)       communications
between Ms. Harrington and her lawyer that fall within the future crimes
exception;

(b)       communications
over which Ms. Harrington has waived solicitor-client privilege during
this proceeding; and

(c)        documents not protected
by solicitor-client privilege that ought to have been disclosed.

I
will deal with each of these categories in turn.

A.        Communications Falling
under the Future Crimes Exception

[
31
]

In this
section, I set out my findings of fact and determination of Mr. McDermott’s
application concerning the future crimes exception to solicitor-client
privilege.

[
32
]

Mr. McDermott
wishes to admit into evidence at trial several documents, and to compel
production of others, that comprise communications between Ms. Harrington and
her sister, and Ms. Harrington and her lawyer, divulging her plan to
“provoke” an adverse ruling concerning her obligation to deliver sworn
responses to outstanding interrogatories in order to launch an appeal that
would result in a delay of the trial. He argues that those communications are
not privileged because they contemplate future conduct that is an abuse of the
process of the Court.

[
33
]

The
history behind this part of Mr. McDermott’s application began in June 2011
when Mr. McDermott served an application to compel Ms. Harrington to
answer interrogatories. Ms. Harrington opposed the application. She
delivered a response to that effect in early July 2011, without any supporting
affidavit materials. Thereafter, on July 15, 2011, during a hearing in Court, she
agreed to answer the interrogatories by August 31, 2011 and consented to a
formal order to that effect. The order was entered in September 2011.

[
34
]

Ms. Harrington
subsequently delivered sworn answers to the interrogatory questions. Shortly
thereafter, Mr. McDermott complained that her responses were in many
instances incomplete and overall, generally inadequate. He filed a further
application on November 17, 2011 to compel answers to questions not answered. Ms. Harrington
opposed the application at first, but she subsequently filed a further
affidavit purporting to provide more complete answers to some but not all of
the outstanding questions. She objected to the relevance of the questions she
did not answer, even though they were related to allegations pleaded in Mr. McDermott’s
counterclaim and even though Ms. Harrington had abandoned her application
to strike it.

[
35
]

The
impugned interrogatory questions sought financial information from Ms. Harrington.
Mr. McDermott’s interrogatory questions were rooted in his concern that Ms. Harrington
was not making accurate disclosure of her income, debt, and expenses. He has pursued
production of complete and accurate financial statements on an ongoing basis.
Some of the interrogatory questions sought clarification of Ms. Harrington’s
property tax and property insurance obligations and what she had said were
loans from her parents in her sworn Form 8 financial statements delivered over
the years. Mr. McDermott was concerned that Ms. Harrington was
significantly overstating and, in some cases, misstating her expense and debt
obligations. Mr. McDermott challenged the accuracy of those stated
obligations.

[
36
]

The
impugned interrogatory questions are relevant to allegations raised in the
pleadings (e.g., her new claim for future extraordinary expenses and liability
for the costs of the access regime). For example, in his amended counterclaim, Mr. McDermott
pleaded at para. 159:

Reasons for judgment quoted by the
Court of Appeal state that any costs the plaintiff spent on access spent would
come at the expense of her other necessary payments and would not be in the
best interests of the children. However, they did not know about the deferred
income, over $120,000 hidden with the Plaintiff's parents, and the fact that
yearly expenses for over $10,000 for mortgage, insurance and property were only
paper payments that were NEVER made.

That
allegation and others of a like nature were denied by Ms. Harrington in
her response pleading. Yet, during her cross-examination on the instant
applications, Ms. Harrington admitted that she does not pay some of the
expenses that she has claimed are ongoing monthly obligations and debts in her
financial statements (delivered in this proceeding for several years),
including a $500 per month debt payment to her parents and taxes and insurance.

[
37
]

Mr. McDermott
continued to pursue his request for answers to his interrogatories. Despite Ms. Harrington’s
opposition, Mr. Maynard later wrote to Mr. McDermott and the Court on
March 30, 2012, with Ms. Harrington’s knowledge, confirming that she would
answer all of the outstanding interrogatory questions.

[
38
]

On
April 17, 2012, a day before a trial management conference (“TMC”) was
scheduled to be heard in this proceeding, Mr. Maynard re-confirmed Ms. Harrington’s
position that she would answer the outstanding interrogatories by May 11,
2012, which was the date they had been promised.

[
39
]

Mr. McDermott
was so distrustful of Ms. Harrington by that date, however, that he asked
for an order at the TMC conducted the next day, on April 18, that her lawyer
scan and email to him the next day a copy of the filed response to his
application.

[
40
]

Ms. Harrington
did not deliver the responses to the outstanding interrogatories by May 11.
When Mr. McDermott followed up with Mr. Maynard to find out when they
would be delivered, Mr. Maynard advised Mr. McDermott, in an email
sent on May 15, 2012, that Ms. Harrington had changed her mind and would
not be answering the outstanding interrogatories. He wrote:

I
confirm receipt of your email.

I also wish you to note that we will
not be making a further response to your interrogatories. As you know I
consider your requests to be irrelevant and your desire to examine the
financial matters that took place ten years ago to be completely ridiculous and
not at all related to the issues before the court. I do have some further
disclosure to send you which I will attempt to get to you either this pm or
tomorrow am. But I will not be making a further response to the interrogatories
as Ii [sic] feel that the responses to date are adequate and there is really
nothing Susan can do to add to them.

[
41
]

What
then had occurred to cause the change in position? It will become clear as I
review the evidence - in particular, the email sent by Ms. Harrington to
her sister and email communications between Ms. Harrington and her lawyer
- that Ms. Harrington had decided that she would force Mr. McDermott
to proceed with his application and that she would deliberately lose it in order
to launch an appeal to delay the trial, all for her own advantage.

[
42
]

Mr. McDermott
has been consistent in his position throughout interlocutory proceedings that Ms. Harrington
continued in her failure to provide proper responses to the interrogatories.
Further, he correctly points out that the interrogatory questions have never
changed.

[
43
]

Mr. McDermott
secured a hearing date for his interrogatories application for May 22, 2012. He
had to chase Ms. Harrington to deliver a filed response to his application
so that he could prepare his application record in accordance with the
Supreme
Court Family Rules
(“
Rules
”). Neither Ms. Harrington nor Mr. Maynard
complied with the order made on April 17 requiring that her filed response to
his application be scanned and served upon him by April 18. Mr. McDermott
pursued their lack of compliance with Mr. Maynard through email
communications. He finally received the document on May 18, 2012, four days
before his application was scheduled to be heard.

[
44
]

Mr. McDermott’s
application to compel appropriate sworn answers to interrogatories was heard on
May 22, 2012. Ms. Harrington’s opposition to his application focused to a
large degree on relevance. Following submissions, and at her request for more
time, I ordered that Ms. Harrington provide sworn answers to the
outstanding interrogatories by June 15, 2012. From Ms. Harrington’s
cross-examination on the instant applications, it turns out that she had a
substantial amount, if not all, of the information necessary to provide the
outstanding information by the time the application was heard on May 22.

[
45
]

Immediately
thereafter, Ms. Harrington advised that she would not comply with the
order and that she intended to appeal. Accordingly, Ms. Harrington failed
to deliver them as ordered, although she never sought a stay of proceedings.
Further, she filed a notice of appeal even though she was required to seek
leave to appeal in the circumstances. Mr. McDermott sent statutory and
case law citations to Mr. Maynard, and advised him that his client must
seek a stay, that he had filed an incorrect form with the Court of Appeal, and
that his client needed to pursue a leave application instead. His advice went
unheeded.

[
46
]

Mr. Maynard
wrote the following to Mr. McDermott on May 23, 2012:

I have received instructions to appeal
Mr. Justice Walker’s rulings yesterday. As such we will not be advancing
the trial until the appeal is properly heard.

From
that, Mr. McDermott understood that Ms. Harrington would not be
proceeding to trial until the appeal was heard.

[
47
]

Mr. McDermott
also filed a contempt application that the parties later agreed should be heard
concurrently with the trial (to avoid having Ms. Harrington fly to
Vancouver from Prince Edward Island given the trial was to continue on July 9).

[
48
]

On
their face, the impugned documents that Mr. McDermott seeks to admit into
evidence at trial speak of a plan agreed to by Ms. Harrington that called
for her lawyer to “provoke” an adverse decision of this Court in respect of Mr. McDermott’s
interrogatories application, and then seek to delay the trial while an appeal
of dubious merit was pursued. The documents also set out several different
possible motives for that conduct. They suggest that delay would benefit Ms. Harrington’s
position in the proceeding because: (a) the older child, E., would reach sufficient
age by the time of trial so that she would not be subject to access orders
without her direct consent or participation; (b) Mr. McDermott’s financial
situation would deteriorate such that his opportunities for access in British
Columbia would be jeopardized; (c) his access to his children in British
Columbia in the summer of 2012 would be prevented altogether; and (d) Ms. Harrington
would not have to travel to Vancouver in July 2012 to attend trial.

[
49
]

Some of
the emails that Mr. McDermott saw on November 12, 2012 concern the interrogatories
and the appeal. Several of them are of significance. Again, they concern the
plan to appeal a decision not yet rendered from an application not yet heard.

[
50
]

The
first email is the non-privileged communication that Ms. Harrington sent
to her sister on May 14, 2012. The second is a string of two communications
between Ms. Harrington and her lawyer, Mr. Maynard, sent the day
before on May 13, 2012. Both of those communications pre-date the hearing date
of May 22 for Mr. McDermott’s interrogatories application.

[
51
]

Ms. Harrington’s
email to her sister speaks of a plan to “manipulate” the court process that, if
disclosed, would harm Ms. Harrington’s interests in the case and could
hurt Mr. Maynard professionally. On behalf of Ms. Harrington, her
counsel admitted during the hearing of the instant applications that the email to
her sister is relevant, producible, and admissible at trial. The email reads:

So
please there can be no local chit chat of lawyers and my court stuff, Ex from
Hell, etc. You’ll prob. All meet at some point.... Hopefully it won't be an
issue..... I am just asking for tight lip discretion.....of course I don't want
anyone talking of my situation anywhere but hopefully you understand what I'm
saying. ...

As
well, the idea of trying for an appeal is not conversation either as it’s
really a manipulation of the court rules and procedures that we're trying to
delay trail [sic] ..... and maybe a strike against John professionally..... And
that could really hurt me if it was disclosed
.

It's
one of those things that it if I tell 2 friends, and they tell 2 friends on and
on and on. I guard myself pretty tightly.... So people just want to throw in
their 2 cents. They may express concern that they haven't a vested interest.

[Emphasis added]

[
52
]

The
communications between Ms. Harrington and her lawyer, sent the day before,
follow upon a meeting between Ms. Harrington and Mr. Maynard where
they discussed a plan to delay the trial. In the first email, written by Ms. Harrington,
she instructed Mr. Maynard to “go for the appeal”.

[
53
]

Mr. Maynard’s
response email to his client followed the same day. In it, he advised Ms. Harrington
that he thought that an appeal should delay the trial for some nine months and
that she was unlikely to win it. He also asked Ms. Harrington to provide
the documents requested in the interrogatories in order to “craft” a reply on
her behalf to “provoke” an adverse ruling. He wrote:

I need the interrogatories docs and
will craft your reply to provoke a decision against us on the interrogatories
and then appeal the decision ASAP.

[
54
]

Those
specific emails between Ms. Harrington and Mr. Maynard comprise one
page of the communications between them that Mr. McDermott read on
November 12, 2012. Of the emails that Mr. McDermott printed or forwarded
to himself, and excluding duplication, there are 52 pages of communications
between Ms. Harrington and her lawyer. The number of pages is not a
quantitative measure of the legal advice seen by Mr. McDermott. Most of
those communications consist of pages of strings of emails from Mr. McDermott
to Ms. Harrington or from Mr. McDermott to Mr. Maynard that are
the subject of a discussion, often brief, between Mr. Maynard and Ms. Harrington.
Apart from communications between lawyer and client, Mr. McDermott read approximately
seven pages of email communications between Ms. Harrington and her family
and friends.

[
55
]

I am
satisfied that Ms. Harrington knew that the information sought by Mr. McDermott
in his interrogatories was relevant. He had previously written to her lawyer
pointing out the relevance of the outstanding questions. She was also told as
much by Mr. Maynard in an email sent over a month earlier, on April 1,
2012, instructing her to gather up the information because they would need it
for trial in any event:

Get started on these and I will review
them to and your responses as well. Much of this stuff we will need for trial
so that is why we might as well give it to him.

[
56
]

No reason
has been offered to explain why that advice to Ms. Harrington to provide
the information to Mr. McDermott was not followed. It is clear, however, that
Ms. Harrington continued to resist providing the financial information
sought by Mr. McDermott.

[
57
]

From
the documents and the evidence that she gave in cross-examination on the
instant applications, I am satisfied that Ms. Harrington sought to delay
the trial for a number of reasons:

(a)       to
impede Mr. McDermott’s ability to challenge the veracity of the expenses
and debts she continued to claim on her financial statements;

(b)       to
impede Mr. McDermott’s access to his children in the summer of 2012;

(c)
to remain home with her children in Prince Edward Island as opposed to
having to travel to Vancouver to attend the continued trial in July 2012;

(d)
to allow her oldest child to reach an age where she would not be bound by
future decisions of the Court without her direct participation; and

(e)       in
the hope that Mr. McDermott’s financial situation would deteriorate so
that it would adversely affect his ability to enjoy access with his children.

[
58
]

I must
also say that it is troubling, in view of the April 1, 2012 email discussed
above, that at the hearing of Mr. McDermott’s application on May 22, Mr. Maynard
argued on behalf of his client that the information sought by Mr. McDermott
in the interrogatories was not relevant.

[
59
]

Now
that I have set out my findings of the relevant facts, I turn to my
determination of this portion of the application. The starting point in my
analysis is to set out a summary of the applicable legal authorities.

[
67
]

Solicitor-client
privilege is an important rule of substantive law that is not to be lightly
frittered away because it provides the right to speak candidly and in confidence
with one’s legal advisor:
Descôteaux v. Mierzwinski
,
1982 CanLII 22 (SCC)
,
[1982] 1
S.C.R. 860
at 871,
875 (S.C.C.). It should be interfered with only to the
extent absolutely necessary in order to achieve a just result:
R. v. McLure
,

2001 SCC 14
;
Legal Services Society v. British Columbia (Information and
Privacy Commissioner
),
2003 BCCA 278
at para.
29
.

[
68
]

Not
every item of correspondence passing between a lawyer and client is privileged,
however. Privilege can only be claimed document by document, and each document
must meet the following criteria: a communication between solicitor and client,
which entails the seeking or giving of legal advice, and which is intended to
be confidential:
Solosky v. The Queen
,
1979 CanLII 9 (SCC)
,
[1980] 1 S.C.R. 821
at 837
.

[
69
]

With
respect to the first requirement, as the Manitoba Court of Appeal stated in
Gower
v. Tolko Manitoba Inc.
,
2001 MBCA 11
, privilege attaches broadly to the
continuum of communications and meetings in which the solicitor tenders advice:

19        ... [T]he communication must
be connected to obtaining legal advice, but legal advice is not confined to
merely telling the client the state of the law. It includes advice as to
what should be done in the relevant legal context. It must, as a
necessity, include ascertaining or investigating the facts upon which the
advice will be rendered. Courts have consistently recognized that
investigation may be an important part of a lawyer’s legal services to a client
so long as they are connected to the provision of those legal services. ...

[
70
]

Where
the claim of privilege is contested, the burden of proof of establishing
privilege over any particular document or communication rests on the person
asserting privilege:
Shooting Star Amusements Ltd. v. Prince George
Agricultural and Historical Association
,
2009 BCCA 452
at para.
7
.
This normally requires something more than counsel’s opinion offered in the
course of argument. But once privilege is established, the onus is on the party
seeking to overcome the privilege to establish that the documentation or
communication should be disclosed:
Camp Development Corporation v. South
Coast Greater Vancouver Transportation Authority,
2011 BCSC 88
at para.
10
.

[
71
]

Privilege
is jealously guarded, but it is not absolute. It has long been recognized that
communications that are obtained to facilitate the commission of a crime or a
fraud are not protected:
Solosky

at 835. This is referred to as the
“future crimes exception”. Privilege never attaches to such communications.

[
72
]

The
future crimes exception encompasses wrongful acts that are not necessarily
criminal in nature. It also applies to torts and abuse of the process of the
court. In
Goldman, Sachs & Co. v. Sessions
,
1999 CanLII 5317 (BC SC)
,
[1999] B.C.J. No. 2815
(S.C.)
at para.
16
, a case involving an alleged abuse of process, Smith J.
(as he then was) held that privilege does not attach to communications in
relation to any intended “unlawful conduct” that causes injury to the legal
rights of other citizens and gives rise to legal remedies, including “breaches
of regulatory statutes, breaches of contract, and torts and other breaches of
duty”. He concluded:

17
It follows, in my
opinion, that professional legal communications obtained to facilitate an abuse
of process are not protected by solicitor-client privilege. The privilege does
not apply because it is no part of a solicitor's professional duties to counsel
a client to misuse the court's process for improper purposes.

18
Moreover, the same result would
be reached on the view that the rule protects all such communications except
those made in furtherance of a crime or fraud. Abuse of process amounts to a
deceit of the court and is of the same order of moral turpitude as civil fraud.
It therefore fits comfortably within the expansive definition of fraud referred
to by Goff J. in
Crescent Farm
,
supra
, at p. 565.

[
73
]

The future crimes exception therefore covers any
“intended unlawful conduct”:
Camp Development
at paras. 22-23;
1784049
Ontario Limited (Alpha Care

Studio 45) v. Toronto (City)
,
2010 ONSC
1204
at paras.
30-36
;
Geographic Resources Integrated Data Solutions
Ltd. v. Peterson
,
2009 CanLII 15436 (ON SC)
, [2009] O.J. No. 1389 at para.
26
(S.C. Master);

Dublin v. Montessori Jewish Day School of Toronto
(2007),
2007 CanLII 8923 (ON SC)
, 85 O.R. (3d)
511 at paras.
42-50
(S.C.J.), leave to appeal granted
[2007] O.J. No. 5230
(S.C.J.)
;
Blue Line Hockey Acquisition Co., Inc. v. Orca Bay Hockey Limited
Partnership
,
2007 BCSC 143
at paras.
31-33
;
Reid v. British
Columbia (Egg and Marketing Board)
,

2006 BCSC 346
at paras.
16-17
;

McIntosh Estates Ltd. v. City of Surrey
,
[1996] B.C.J. No. 2008 (S.C.
Master)
, aff’d (1997),
1997 CanLII 3117 (BC CA)
, 52 B.C.L.R. (3d) 277 (C.A.);
Crescent Farm Sports
Ltd. v. Sterling Officers Ltd.
,

[1967] 1 Ch. D. 553
;
Hallstone
Products Ltd. v. Canada
,
[2004] O.J. No. 496 (S.C. Master)
; and
Majormaki
Holdings v. Wong
,
2007 BCSC 1399
.

[
74
]

Thus, communications
between a lawyer and a client who deliberately uses the lawyer to facilitate
any unlawful conduct is simply not within the proper functional scope of the
privilege.

[
75
]

In
order to make out the “future crimes exception”, three specific elements must
be met: (a) the challenged communications must pertain to proposed future
conduct; (b) the client must be seeking to advance conduct which it knows or
should know is unlawful; and (c) the wrongful conduct being contemplated must
be clearly wrong. These requirements are applied stringently:
Camp
Development
at para. 28.

[
76
]

It is
immaterial whether the lawyer was an unwitting dupe or knowing participant in
providing the advice underlying the wrongful conduct:
Solosky

at
835-836. Rather, the key consideration is the intention and state of mind of
the client at the time the advice was obtained:
Donell v. GJB Enterprises
Inc.
,
2012 BCCA 135
at paras.
69-70
;
Blue Line Hockey
at para.
34.

[
77
]

In addition,
in order to invoke the future crimes exception, the applicant must make out a
prima
facie
case:
Camp Development
at para. 24. Although the relevant
case law speaks of the threshold in varying terms, it is clear that it is
insufficient to merely assert that the lawyer’s advice was sought in
furtherance of an unlawful purpose:
Dublin

at para.
43
. There must
be clear and convincing evidence - that is, something to give colour to the
charge, in light of all the evidence and the surrounding circumstances - that
the client communicated with the lawyer with the intention of committing an
unlawful act, be it criminal or tortious, and that the client knew or ought to
have known that the intended conduct was unlawful:
Dublin

at paras.
42-43
;

Blue Line Hockey
at para. 35, citing
Goldman Sachs
. It is
therefore not absolutely necessary for the court to weigh conflicting evidence
and make findings of fact in order to determine that the exception applies:
Goldman
Sachs
at para. 21.

[
78
]

Lastly,
where the applicant establishes a
prima facie
case, the court must then
review the documents in question “to ascertain whether the exception does in
fact pertain or whether the asserted privilege properly exists”:
Camp
Development
at para. 24.

[
79
]

I have
determined that Mr. McDermott has established, through clear and
convincing evidence, that the future crimes exception is engaged. No privilege

Mr. McDermott has also established a
prima facie
case that the plan
spoken of in the impugned emails was part of a larger plan by Ms. Harrington
to delay the trial.

[
80
]

No
credible evidence has been provided by or on behalf of Ms. Harrington to explain

[
81
]

I wish
to note that Mr. McDermott made it abundantly clear from the very outset
of these applications that he would attempt to establish more than a
prima

case that Ms. Harrington set out to engage in this plan. His

[
82
]

Ms. Harrington
chose not to lead any evidence beyond her own to refute his allegations or
answer his evidence or explain away the clear wording in the impugned emails.
Specifically, she chose not to call any other witnesses (such as Mr. Maynard
or her sister) to explain the impugned emails, including the context in which

[
83
]

I say
all of this because in closing argument, Mr. Maynard suggested it would be
inappropriate for me to find that Mr. McDermott had established, on a

Although he did not say so directly, his submission might be interpreted to
mean that his strategy on this
voir dire
was simply to rebut Mr. McDermott’s
alternative position. In other words, if he had otherwise known that the Court
would consider making a final determination that Ms. Harrington had, in
fact, engaged in the alleged unlawful conduct, he would have led further
evidence and crafted his submissions differently.

[
84
]

I do
not accede to this submission for several reasons.

[
85
]

The
case law speaks of the necessary threshold to engage the future crimes
exception, but it does not hold that it is inappropriate to make a final
determination whether the alleged unlawful conduct was proved on a balance of
probabilities. The case law sets the minimum height of the hurdle that Mr. McDermott
must clear in the first instance, but it does not preclude or prevent him from
going further over that bar.

[
86
]

Ms. Harrington
and her counsel were well aware from the very start of these applications that Mr. McDermott
sought to establish on a balance of probabilities that she devised a plan to
abuse the court process. Ms. Harrington denied the existence of any such
plan and sought to explain the emails in her affidavit and
viva voce

evidence. Her counsel denied the existence of any plan in his opening and
closing submissions, stating that there was no evidence to prove it.

[
87
]

Finally,
when I questioned Mr. Maynard during closing argument about the
appropriateness of the submission he had just made, given his client’s position
throughout Mr. McDermott’s application, he did not point to or say that there
was any other evidence that his client would have tendered to defend Mr. McDermott’s
application. Nor did he say or suggest what other approach his client might
have taken on the application. In the end, Mr. Maynard reverted to his argument
that Ms. Harrington’s evidence constituted a complete answer to Mr. McDermott’s
application.

[
88
]

Ms. Harrington
had notice of and full opportunity to answer the charges against her; she chose
the manner in which to defend them.

[
89
]

In
these circumstances, it is not inappropriate to make a determination that Ms. Harrington
engaged in unlawful conduct.

[
90
]

Moving
on, in light of Ms. Harrington’s allegations that Mr. McDermott
improperly or unlawfully obtained evidence, I must now consider whether the
impugned emails should be admitted and whether all documents concerning the
matters discussed in the impugned emails should be produced, including
solicitor- client communications, or whether I should refrain from making those
orders in view of the manner in which Mr. McDermott obtained access to the
impugned emails.

[
91
]

Traditionally,
courts have followed the general inclusionary rule that the manner of obtaining
relevant evidence, whether by legal or illegal means, will not affect its
admissibility because judges should have all relevant evidence before them: A.
Bryant et al., eds.,
The Law of Evidence in Canada
, 3d ed. (Markham:
LexisNexis Canada Inc., 2009) at §9.1 [
The Law of Evidence
]. If I were
to follow this line of authority, an order for production would follow as a
matter of course.

[
92
]

Recently,
however, where evidence has been obtained unlawfully or surreptitiously, courts
have recognized that there is a limited discretion at common law to exclude
relevant non-privileged evidence, the exercise of which involves “a balancing
of competing interests which can be usefully viewed as assessing the probative
value of the evidence as against its prejudicial effect”:
Mathews v. Mathews
,

2007 BCSC 1825
at para.
43
. See also:
R. v. G.J.
,
2012 ONSC 5413 (CanLII)
,
[2012] O.J. No. 4462
(S.C.J.)
;
Biehl v. Strang
,
2011 BCSC 1373
;
S.C. v. J.C.
,
2009
SKQB 87
;
Rawlek v. Rawlek
,
[2003] B.C.J. No. 2231 (S.C.)
;
B.
(A.D.) v. B. (E.)
,
[1997] B.C.J. No. 227 (S.C.)
;
Sweeton v. Sweeton
,

1996 CanLII 2972 (BC SC)
,
[1996] B.C.J. No. 3138 (Master)
;
Seddon v. Seddon
,
[1994] B.C.J. No. 1729
(S.C.)
.

[
93
]

In
Mathews
,
Mr. Justice Barrow considered the potential prejudicial effect from
several perspectives, which approach was most recently adopted by Veale J. in
B.D.C.
v. B.J.B.
,
2012 YKSC 64
. At para. 11, he summarized the various forms
of prejudice a court must consider in the following manner:

1.
Prejudice to the party opposing the admission of the evidence: Prejudice may be
found if the evidence is of uncertain provenance, is incomplete or capable of
manipulation. ...

2.
Prejudice to the trial process: Prejudice may be found where the cost of
admitting the evidence is out of proportion to its probative value. In two
precedent cases, the sheer volume of recorded material made the taped evidence
inadmissible (i.e. 20 hours of tape recording in
Seddon v. Seddon
,

[1994] B.C.J. No. 1729 (S.C.)
, and recordings made over a period of three
and a half years in
Rawlek v. Rawlek
,
[2003] B.C.J. No. 2231
(S.C.)
).

3.
Prejudice to the administration of justice: Where, for example, the secret
interception of a private communication is a criminal offence.
Section 184(1)

of the
Criminal Code

makes it an indictable offence to intercept a
private communication “by means of any electro-magnetic, acoustic, mechanical
or other device.”
In
Mathews
, the diary and card were not obtained in a
manner that constituted a criminal offence. Indeed, the diary and the card
would have been required to be produced in a List of Documents or on request at
an examination for discovery.

4. Prejudice that would arise by
excluding the evidence: As Barrow J. stated at para. 56, there is little
doubt that the exclusion of evidence that is reliable and shows physical abuse
of a child, for example, would harm the reputation of the administration of
justice. ...

[
94
]

I have
determined that the impugned emails concerning the plan, including the appeal
and answers to the interrogatories, should be admitted and that all documents,
including emails, notes, and memoranda relating to those matters, must be
produced. I make this ruling for the following reasons.

[
95
]

To
begin with, I reject Ms. Harrington’s assertion that Mr. McDermott
hacked his way into her computer to read her emails. She has not proved that to
be the case.

[
96
]

I
accept Mr. McDermott’s evidence concerning the manner in which he obtained

[
97
]

Essentially,
Mr. McDermott says that on November 12, 2012, he was carrying out computer

[
98
]

At
first, he thought he had accessed Ms. Harrington’s general AOL home page containing

[
99
]

Mr. McDermott
was astonished at the contents of that email because it confirmed what he had

believed that the impugned email between Ms. Harrington and her sister
confirmed her ongoing attempts to ignore court orders when it suited her

[
100
]

Mr. McDermott
then decided to search several search terms in her mailbox to see if he could
locate any other emails referring to delay and the trial. In carrying out those

[
101
]

It
became apparent during cross examination on the instant applications that Ms. Harrington’s

security question. Ms. Harrington was asked to enter onto a laptop
supplied by court services, which contained no data or programs on it other

home page appeared on the monitor even though she did not enter a password or
answer a security question. She was then asked to click on an icon to enter her
own email account. Although Ms. Harrington thought she would have to enter
a password or answer a security question once she did so, that was not the

[
102
]

A
number of reasons for how this could happen were raised during argument. For
example, it was postulated that since Ms. Harrington had used the court
laptop the day before to access her AOL account to answer questions, the
browser had remembered her password and account information. No evidence was
tendered to support that submission or any of the other possibilities that were
offered.

[
103
]

A
number of possible explanations were also raised during argument for the reason(s)
why the Google search carried out by Mr. McDermott on November 12, 2012 displayed
a link directly into Ms. Harrington’s AOL email account. One possibility
is that a web browser on Ms. Harrington’s home computer operated in a
manner that allowed her AOL account to be picked up by the Google search

office supply store for repairs and diagnostic checks on several occasions
prior to November 12, 2012. Lastly, Ms. Harrington also accesses her AOL

was suggested that Ms. Harrington’s email account was open to access
because someone using either computer had inadvertently left her AOL account open
and running within the computer while accessing a different site on the
internet. In the end, however, all of those possibilities are postulations not
supported by expert evidence, let alone proved from the actual evidence adduced
on the applications.

[
104
]

I do
wish to say at this juncture that I do not accept Ms. Harrington’s evidence
that her children have never had access to her AOL email account. In attempting
to explain why a particularly nasty email from a friend about Mr. McDermott
(and what should be done with him) was sent to Ms. Harrington’s brother’s
email account as opposed to her own AOL account, it became clear to me that
this was done in order to avoid the children reading the comments. It is also
clear that Ms. Harrington knows that her children have had access, perhaps
unauthorized, to her AOL email account in the past.

[
105
]

Apart
from two or three other emails between Ms. Harrington and her sister that
he read, I am satisfied that Mr. McDermott has provided copies of all of
the emails that he read on November 12, 2012. I accept his evidence that he did
not read any other emails between Ms. Harrington and Mr. Maynard
other than those he has produced. He has not gained access to Ms. Harrington’s
communications with Mr. Maynard about any other matter aside from those
disclosed in the impugned emails. He has not accessed or read their privileged
communications concerning any other aspect of their trial or case strategy.

[
106
]

In
reaching my decision to order production, I have considered the factors set out
in the case law. In this case, Ms. Harrington has not disputed that these
emails in evidence are true copies, nor has she argued that they were
manipulated in any way. The information sought by Mr. McDermott in the
interrogatories was relevant to issues to be determined at trial, which Ms. Harrington
knew. Unlike
Rawleck
and
Seddon
, there are only a small number of
documents in issue. The emails demonstrate a concerted effort by Ms. Harrington
to engage in a course of conduct that she understood to be an abuse of the
process of the Court in order to achieve a number of distinct advantages to Mr. McDermott’s
detriment. In addition, I fail to see how it can be in the best interests of
the children to delay the determination of their access regime with their father,
particularly as they are now in their teenage years, while Ms. Harrington
pursues a tactic aimed at manipulating the process of the Court for her own
advantage. As a matter of trial fairness, the impugned emails should be
admitted into evidence.

[
107
]

I have
also considered, as one of many factors, Ms. Harrington’s admission that
she has in the past intentionally accessed and read private communications
between Mr. McDermott and their son without their knowledge. While giving

B.        Waiver of
Privilege

1.         Introductory
Remarks and Case Law

[
110
]

I turn
now to consider whether Ms. Harrington has waived privilege over other
subject matters during the course of this proceeding. It is useful to set out a
brief summary of the law before I provide my findings and my determination.

[
111
]

As I
have already pointed out, solicitor-client privilege will not be lightly
interfered with, but privilege can be waived in certain circumstances. Waiver
of privilege may, of course, be express or implied.

[
112
]

Courts
have moved away from the proposition that privilege may be lost through
inadvertence. Under the modern common law, generally privilege may be waived in
civil cases only by the client, and then only when it is waived deliberately
and knowingly or through implication, but not inadvertently:
Le Soleil Hotel
& Suites Ltd. v. Le Soleil Management Inc.
,
2007 BCSC 1420
at para.
21
,
citing
Somerville Belkin Industries Ltd. v. Brocklesby Transport

(1985),

1985 CanLII 563 (BC SC)
,
65 B.C.L.R. 260 (S.C.)
. According to McLachlin J. (as she then was), in certain
circumstances waiver may also “occur in the absence of an intention to waive,
where fairness and consistency so require”:
S & K. Processors Ltd. v.
Campbell Avenue Herring Producers Ltd.
(1983),
1983 CanLII 407 (BC SC)
,
45 B.C.L.R. 218
at 220 (S.C.)
.

[
113
]

Accordingly, waiver may be
inferred when a party discloses so much information on a subject that, as a
matter of fairness and consistency, that party cannot be permitted to elect to
withhold the remainder:
The Law of Evidence
at §14.128. This basis for
waiver was discussed in
Fording Coal Ltd. v. United Steelworkers of America,
Local Union No. 7384

(1998),
1998 CanLII 6613 (BC SC)
,
65 B.C.L.R. (3d) 236 (S.C.)
at para.
19

in the following manner:

Case authority supports the
proposition that a party may not use solicitor-client privilege as a means of
selectively putting evidence before the court or as a defence that the other
side cannot inquire into. For example, where a party has put into evidence part
of a privileged memorandum, the court may order that the rest of the memorandum
also be entered into evidence:
Great Atlantic Insurance Co. v. Home
Insurance Co. and others
,
[1981] 2 All E.R. 485 (Eng. C.A.)
. Similarly,
where a witness has testified as to the contents of a privileged communication
at trial, fairness requires that the communication itself be produced:
York
v. Gilligan
,
(1996),
1996 CanLII 823 (BC SC)
,
19 B.C.LR. (3d) 40 (B.C. Master)
. In such cases, the
“waiver” of solicitor-client privilege arises because equity demands it, not
because there has been an intentional waiver by the party asserting the
privilege. ...

[
114
]

In addition, an intentional
waiver over parts of privileged documents (or “cherry picking”, as it is called
in some of the cases) cannot be used to prevent broader disclosure where the
court would otherwise be misled or where unfairness would result. In
Stevens
v. Canada (Prime Minister)
,
1998 CanLII 9075 (FCA)
,
[1998] 4 F.C. 89 (C.A.)
, at para.
51
, the
Federal Court of Appeal stated:

With respect to
the release of portions of the records, a similar view has been adopted in
British Columbia. In
Lowry v. Can. Mountain Holidays Ltd.
[(1984),
1984 CanLII 378 (BC SC)
, 59
B.C.L.R. 137 at 143 (S.C.)], Finch J. emphasized that all the circumstances must
be taken into consideration and that the conduct of the party and the presence
of an intent to mislead the court or another litigant are of primary
importance.

[
115
]

Therefore,
parties may not disclose portions or a subset of an ongoing series of
communications without disclosing all of the communications which relate to
that same subject matter:
Camp Development
at para. 74.

[
116
]

In
addition, privilege is waived by a party which, by its own pleadings or during
the proceedings, puts in issue its state of mind or the nature of legal advice
it received:
G.W.L. Properties v. W.K. Grace and Co. of Canada
(1992),
10 C.P.C. (3d) at 169-170 (B.C.S.C.). But a party cannot be said to have waived
privilege only because the other party made allegations “as to a state of affairs
on which a party may have received legal advice”:
Doman Forest Products Ltd.
v. GMAC Commercial Credit Corp. - Canada
,
2004 BCCA 512
at para.
19
.

[
117
]

When
privilege is waived, the question then becomes to what extent. In
Souter v.
375561 B.C. Ltd
.
(1995),
1995 CanLII 843 (BC CA)
,
15 B.C.L.R. (3d) 213 (C.A.)
at paras.
24-25
,
the court rejected the proposition that a loss of privilege over one aspect of
a client’s file would result in a complete loss of privilege as between the
client and its lawyers. Rather, as already stated, privilege is waived only
with respect to materials pertaining to the specific subject matter in
question:
W. Johnston Equities Ltd. v. Allen
,
2012 BCSC 414
at para.
29
.
Thus, the existence and extent of any waiver is a question of fact to be
determined according to its relevance to the matters at issue:
Biehl
at paras.
64-74
,
and the authorities cited in the case report.

[
118
]

Rule  9-1(17) of the
Rules
,
which uses the same language as Supreme Court Civil Rule 7-1(20), provides a
mechanism to determine whether documents fall within the ambit of the waiver of
privilege:

If, on an application for production
of a document, production is objected to on the grounds of privilege, the court
may inspect the document for the purpose of deciding the validity of the objection.

[
119
]

There is some debate over
how the court should exercise its discretion under this Rule. In
Keefer
Laundry v. Pellerin Milnor Corp.
,
2006 BCSC 1180
at paras.
73-75
,
which involved the similarly worded predecessor to Rule 7-1(20), Gray J.
cautioned against the court undertaking a review simply for the convenience of
the parties. She said, at para. 73, that it is most appropriate for the court
to review the documents only when the party seeking to establish privilege cannot
do so without revealing the privileged information itself.

. A similar

No. 1687 (C.A.)

]

The

[

In
situations where privileged communications come into possession of a third
party by improper means, courts have recently relied upon notions of public
policy precluding a party who has acted improperly in the proceedings from
using that evidence. In particular, although courts have long followed
Calcraft
v. Guest
,
[1898] 1 Q.B. 759
C.A. - which suggests that privilege is lost
whether the disclosure is by accident or by design, and thus privileged
material may be admitted at trial if not restrained by an injunction beforehand
- the more recent trend in the authorities is to enquire into the circumstances
by which the privileged information has come to the attention of the third
party:
Airst v. Airst
,
1998 CanLII 14647 (ON CTGD)
,
[1998] O.J. No. 2615
(C.J. (Gen. Div.)) at para. 14;

Miller v. Miller
,
2000 ABQB 12
;
Eizenshtein v. Eizenshtein
,

2008 CanLII 31808 (ON SC)
,
[2008] O.J. No. 2600
at paras.
11-12
;
Pottruff v. Don Berry
,

2012 ONSC 311
; and
Biehl
. Accordingly, in weighing the public interest
that the truth should be ascertained against the public interest that a
solicitor should be able to deal with the client confidentially (without fear
that their communications will be intercepted by stealth or trick and then used
against the client in evidence), courts have held that privileged material
obtained by improper conduct should not be disclosed.

[
184
]

In
Eizenshtein

at para.
45
, Wildman J. provided a non-exhaustive list of some of the
factors that a court might consider in making a determination whether
privileged material improperly obtained should be admitted into court
proceedings over the objection of the client: (a) whether the evidence is
relevant to an issue before the court; (b) whether a principled analysis of the
circumstances of disclosure requires, in fairness, that the material be
disclosed; and (c) whether the probative value of the evidence outweighs the
prejudicial effect of admitting it. At para. 32, he explained the
overriding concern in these applications, stating that the “court is required
to conduct an inquiry to determine, in all the circumstances, whether the
information is so important to the outcome of the case that it should be
admitted despite the existence of the privilege”.

[

V.        Ms. Harrington’s Mistrial
Application

[
236
]

Ms. Harrington
submits that as a result of the interception of the various email communications
between her and Mr. Maynard, Mr. McDermott has purposefully gained
knowledge of her trial strategy, trial evidence, and trial planning, causing
her to suffer “extreme” prejudice. She says that taking into consideration all
of the circumstances here, the prejudice cannot be redressed or cured and the
only remedy available is a mistrial.

[
237
]

Mr. McDermott
opposes Ms. Harrington’s application, stating that she has suffered
minimal prejudice, if any, and that a mistrial is not necessary or appropriate
in the circumstances.

[
238
]

In support of her position
that a mistrial is the appropriate remedy in this case, Ms. Harrington has
referred me to
Sawridge First Nation v. Congress of Aboriginal Peoples
,

2007 FC 657
, which provides a correct statement of the law. In that case, after
considering several authorities, the court summarized the general principles
relating to the granting of a mistrial:

[407]
Assuming that I have jurisdiction, it seems to me that, from the cases
cited, the principles that should guide me on the mistrial issue are as
follows:

1. The
decision to grant a mistrial in the present case is discretionary;

2. In
exercising that discretion, should I consider whether, in all of the
circumstances of the case, a mistrial is needed to prevent a miscarriage of
justice and whether the facts and arguments placed before me disclose a real
danger of prejudice or miscarriage of justice or, at the very least, a
reasonable possibility of prejudice to the Plaintiffs;

3. I should bear in mind that a
mistrial is extraordinary relief and that, even if I think that prejudice has
occurred, before granting the remedy, I should allow other options to be
canvassed to see if the trial can be saved in a way that is just and fair in
the circumstances.

[
239
]

Thus, a
mistrial is discretionary relief that is granted only in drastic circumstances
when a trial judge determines that there are no remedies available that will
preserve the fairness of trial or prevent a miscarriage of justice. Put another
way, this relief should be granted only when the trial judge concludes that
there is a reasonable apprehension that either party will not have a fair trial
if the trial continues, but that a fair trial would be possible if it began
anew before a different judge.

[
240
]

Given
the extraordinary nature of granting a mistrial, a strong case must be
presented to the court before mistrial can be directed. Further, in the face of
any irregularities, the trial judge must canvass all options to determine
whether the trial can be saved:
Carey v. Ontario
,
[1991] O.J. No. 1819
(C.A.)
. The cost in delay of having a new trial is also a factor to consider:
Dayton
v. Barr
,
2005 BCSC 591
at para.
21
.

[
241
]

These principles were
echoed by Low J. in
de Araujo v. Read
,
2004 BCCA 267
, who, dissenting in
outcome only, stated:

[100]    The
hardship and expense, both public and private, that a new trial inevitably
occasions afford a further policy reason for such deference. The comments
of Meredith J.A. in
Caswell v. Toronto R.W. Co.

(1911),
24 O.L.R. 339
at
350-51 (C.A.)
, which are set out at para. 55 of my colleague’s reasons and
which I will repeat for emphasis, express this point:

A new trial is a hardship under any circumstances; and
when granted upon insufficient grounds is a very grave injustice; to take away
from any one that which has been fairly won, and to subject him to the delay
and cost, and the mental and physical strain, of another trial, as well as to
the uncertainty of its outcome, is something which fairly may be thought
intolerable. New trials are, of course, occasionally necessary in order that
justice may be done between the parties, but they are contrary to the public
interests, and may fairly be described as necessary evils, when necessary...

A
strong case must, therefore, be presented before a new trial can properly be
directed...

[
242
]

I consider that cases may
arise where the court is unable to disabuse itself of the persuasive effect of
inadmissible and highly prejudicial evidence, such that its ability to give the
parties a fair trial has been impaired. As Mr. McDermott points out,
however, judges are frequently required to rule upon the admissibility of
documents or statements in the criminal context. Yet, despite being exposed to
such material, as the court
noted in
R. v. Novak
,
1995 CanLII 2024 (BC CA)
,
[1995] B.C.J. No. 1127 (C.A.)
at para.
8
,
judges are accustomed to ignoring inadmissible evidence when rendering a
decision:

Judges are routinely called upon to
disabuse their minds of evidence which they have heard but which, as a matter
of law, is not admissible in the trial before them. It is fundamental to
their role to decide the case only on the evidence properly admissible in that
case...

See
also
Dobranski v. Dobranski
,
[1998] B.C.J. No. 295 (C.A.)
at para. 26
;

R. v. McIntyre
,
[1984] B.C.J. No. 1296 (Co. Ct.)
at para. 8
.

[
243
]

There
is no basis to order a mistrial in this case. The emails protected by
solicitor-client privilege that Mr. McDermott reviewed do not disclose any
of Ms. Harrington’s trial strategy. Further, the matters discussed in them
are benign in comparison to the subject matters over which Ms. Harrington
has intentionally waived privilege during these proceedings, including through the
trial.

[
244
]

The
most that can be said of the limited number of emails Mr. McDermott found
on November 12, 2012 is they reveal that (a) Mr. Maynard suggested how Ms. Harrington
should respond to Mr. McDermott, including the specific words to use; (b) derogatory
comments were made about Mr. McDermott by Ms. Harrington, her family
and friends, and Mr. Maynard; (c) a court proceeding was scheduled to take
place; (d) Mr. McDermott’s relationship with his children, including some
of his telephone conversations with them, was discussed; (e) Ms. Harrington
was displeased with Mr. Maynard for sending a privileged email communication
to Mr. McDermott; (f) Ms. Harrington discussed part of her travel
plans to British Columbia; and (g) Ms. Harrington questioned the dollar
amounts of some of Mr. Maynard’s accounts. I am satisfied that any
prejudice Ms. Harrington may have suffered from Mr. McDermott’s
review of these privileged emails is minimal and does not require amelioration
by terms.

[
245
]

To the
contrary, Mr. McDermott has suffered prejudice because the emails that he found
on November 12, 2012 demonstrate that Ms. Harrington has failed to honour
her disclosure obligations under the
Rules
and that she planned to
manipulate the Court’s process for her advantage.

[
246
]

Moreover,
Ms. Harrington’s affidavit evidence that her primary means of communications
with her lawyer was by email was shown to be unreliable in cross-examination.
She admitted to having meetings and telephone calls with her lawyer to discuss
substantive matters. Yet she claimed to have no recollection whatsoever of the
number of them, not even an approximation. She could not even remember those
that occurred over the last three weeks. I am satisfied that the basis for Mr. Harrington’s
statements in her affidavits is her unhappiness that Mr. McDermott
accessed her emails, and not anything of substance.

[
247
]

Finally,
a mistrial would not be in the best interests of the children. I say that for
two reasons.

[
248
]

First, Mr. McDermott
has, thus far in the trial, established through the evidence of psychologist
and s. 15 expert, Dr. Elterman, a
prima facie
case that the
children show signs of parental alienation resulting in part from their
circumstances in Prince Edward Island. Dr. Elterman also opined that it is
important for the children to have an ongoing relationship with their father
and that it was important for them to have access with him in Vancouver. He
expressed the following opinions in his s. 15 reports:

In
considering this case I have entertained two hypotheses and these are that it
is the distance and the children's experience with Mr McDermott that has led to
their reluctance to visit. The other hypothesis is that it is the general
anxiety and worry about the access visits that comes from the atmosphere at Ms. Harrington's
home that has led to the children developing a negative attitude towards visits
or that they have come to conclude that it is just too complicated for them to
have a relationship with both parents. As I see it, the evidence supports the
second hypothesis more than the first. While the comments that Ms. Harrington
may have made to the children are intended as supportive, they have come to be
interpreted over a long period of time as expressing a foreboding and a period
where their mother worries about their safety. It is more likely than not that
[B.’s] anxiety symptoms relate to this situation rather than an abusive or problematic
experience at Mr. McDermott.

...
It is not good enough for Ms Harrington to take the attitude that the children
can either go or not go [to Vancouver] and that it is up to them to decide. I
believe that she has had a role in the problem that has developed over the
years and she needs to be part of the solution. Both male and female children
benefit from having a relationship with a father as fathers provide something
quite different to the type of parenting provided by a mother. Ms. Harrington's
over-involvement with the children's access and relationship with Mr. McDermott
is not unlike the parent who brings the child to my office door and says to the
child "I will be right outside the door and if you yell I will be right
in". The message that these situations convey is that there is something
to be anxious about. The children need to be sent with the attitude that they
will have a good time and their mother values the relationship that the
children have with their father. I note that one of Ms. Harrington's
collaterals made a remark that she needs to let it go and move on and that
there is still too much anger. It may be of benefit to Ms Harrington to seek
some counseling for herself in terms of letting go of the fight which she
perhaps sees as protecting the children but has in reality, made their lives
more complicated.

...

The second question is "whether
there is any treatment or intervention required to assist the children".
The answer is "no". The interventions thus far [referring to those in
Prince Edward Island] have, in my opinion, worked from the assumption that they
have to advocate from the position of the children's stated wishes. These
wishes were the result of maternal and other influence and may not be what the
children genuinely wish. As a consequence, these interventions may have
actually been counter-productive. The best "treatment" for the
children is to continue visiting. I interviewed the children in Vancouver in
August 2011 and they had had a good vacation but nonetheless felt the need to
express their desire not to visit in a half-hearted formulaic way.

[
249
]

It is
also important to keep in mind that even though the instant applications are
brought mid-trial before Ms. Harrington has put in her case, it cannot be
overlooked that she does not intend to call any expert or treating health care
professional to rebut any of Dr. Elterman’s evidence.

[
250
]

Second,
there is no basis to conclude that if a mistrial is ordered, the parties could
or would agree to the terms of an access regime in Vancouver that would be adhered
to. They have not been able to do so over the past eleven years. Mr. McDermott
has established a
prima facie
case at trial that Ms. Harrington did
not comply with court orders concerning the access regime on a number of
occasions, forcing Mr. McDermott to threaten and pursue contempt
proceedings. Mr. McDermott also obtained an admission from Ms. Harrington
during the hearing of the instant applications that she did not always comply with

were, to her own mind, in the best interests of the children, she admitted that
she did not seek to vary terms of court-ordered access even though she knew
that Mr. McDermott insisted that they be followed. In essence, she acted
unilaterally.

[
251
]

There
is no possibility that the parties will be able to reach an agreement
concerning Mr. McDermott’s access to his children in Vancouver that will
be complied with. Accordingly, a mistrial would not be in the best interests of
the children.

[
252
]

In
conclusion, there is no merit to the mistrial application and I would dismiss
it.
